pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Current, voltage, and what they measure

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum):** KS3 Physics, 'Electricity and electromagnetism / Current electricity' — statutory wording 'electric current, measured in amperes, in circuits, series and parallel circuits, currents add where branches meet and current as flow of charge' and 'potential difference, measured in volts, battery and bulb ratings; resistance, measured in ohms, as the ratio of potential difference (p.d.) to current' (verified by fetch).

- **Standards — US National (NGSS):** there is NO middle-school performance expectation covering DC-circuit current/voltage analysis — circuits are not an NGSS MS topic — so this topic is UK-ANCHORED (the nearest NGSS contact, MS-PS2-3, concerns electromagnet/motor force strength, not circuit quantities). State the UK anchor honestly and note NGSS does not cover it at MS.

- **Operational details:** This topic QUANTIFIES the circuit by naming two distinct quantities that beginners notoriously fuse. Current is the RATE OF FLOW OF CHARGE (amperes, measured by an ammeter placed IN SERIES); potential difference / voltage is the ENERGY TRANSFERRED PER UNIT CHARGE (volts, measured by a voltmeter placed IN PARALLEL across a component). The single most important teaching job is to separate these three things — charge (the stuff that flows), current (how fast it flows), and voltage/energy (what the cell gives each bit of charge and what each component takes) — because almost every later electricity error comes from blurring them. The most effective route is a concrete transport model (a moving loop of 'charge' that the cell energises and that drops energy at components) so 'current is the same all the way round' and 'voltage is a difference ACROSS something' become visible rather than asserted.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional / early-formal, ~11–12). At KS2 the child watched 'more cells → brighter bulb' qualitatively.
bestPractices: Separate the three ideas explicitly and keep saying them: CHARGE is the stuff that flows, CURRENT is how fast it flows (rate of flow of charge, amperes), VOLTAGE is the energy each unit of charge carries/delivers (energy per charge, volts). Most errors are a collapse of these into one 'electricity'.

Use a transport/loop model so current-is-conserved is seen, not told: a moving loop of charge (the rope-loop kinaesthetic, or an animated charge ring) where every part moves together — push anywhere and the whole loop moves — makes 'current is the same all the way round a series circuit' immediate and kills the current-used-up error.

Model voltage as energy GIVEN to charge by the cell and TAKEN from charge by components: charges leave the cell 'loaded' and 'unload' energy at the bulb. This grounds 'energy per charge' and explains why voltage is always measured ACROSS two points, not at one point.

Drill the meter rules with the reason, not as a ritual: an ammeter goes IN SERIES because it counts the charge passing through (it must be in the flow); a voltmeter goes IN PARALLEL because it compares the energy of charge on either side of a component (it measures a difference across).

Treat analogies with explicit caveats: the water-circuit / central-heating model (pump = cell, flow rate = current, pressure/push = voltage) helps, but flag where it breaks (water can leak; charge cannot leave the wire; the pipe is always full). Pair it with the rope loop, which is strong for current but silent on energy.

Contrast 'the battery provides voltage, the circuit determines the current' — the cell does not push out a fixed current; current depends on what the charge meets around the loop. This pre-empts 'the battery supplies X amps no matter what'.

Anchor in measurement: have pupils predict, then read, ammeters at several points (all equal in a series loop) and voltmeters across the cell and across each component (they share out), so the abstract definitions are tied to instrument readings.
keyRepresentations: The moving charge-loop / rope-loop model — a continuous loop that all moves together when pushed anywhere; current = how fast the loop moves (same everywhere in series), with the cell as the hand doing the pushing.
Charges as energy carriers — little parcels leave the cell 'full' and 'empty out' energy at each component, making voltage = energy per charge and a DIFFERENCE across a component.
Ammeter-in-series vs voltmeter-in-parallel circuit diagram — the ammeter in the line of flow, the voltmeter bridging across a component, each annotated with what it counts.
The water-circuit / central-heating analogy (with caveats) — pump = cell, flow rate = current (A), pressure/push = potential difference (V).
A multi-point readout circuit — several ammeters around a series loop reading identically, and voltmeters across cell and components showing the pd sharing out.
commonMisconceptions: Current is 'used up' as it goes round — carried over from KS2; in a series circuit the current is the SAME everywhere, and an ammeter reads identically before and after the bulb (the bulb takes energy, not charge).
Conflating current and voltage — saying 'voltage flows through' the circuit; voltage is not a flow, it is the energy per charge / a difference across two points, while current is the flow.
Treating voltage as a property of a single point rather than a difference ACROSS two points — hence the voltmeter must straddle a component, not sit at one spot.
Believing the battery delivers a fixed current regardless of the circuit — the cell sets the voltage; the current depends on the whole loop (and its resistance).
Thinking charge is created or consumed — charge is conserved and simply circulates; the cell transfers energy to it, it does not manufacture or destroy the charge.
Putting the ammeter in parallel or the voltmeter in series — a symptom of not knowing that one counts through-flow (series) and the other measures a difference across (parallel).
Assuming more current automatically means more voltage — they are distinct quantities; their relationship depends on resistance (the next topic).

learn.summary: Help 11–12 year-olds separate three ideas they tend to fuse into one 'electricity': CHARGE (the stuff that flows), CURRENT (how fast it flows — rate of flow of charge, amperes, measured by an ammeter IN SERIES), and VOLTAGE/potential difference (energy transferred per unit charge, volts, measured by a voltmeter IN PARALLEL across a component). Centre the work on a circuit model with visibly flowing charge, measurement at multiple points, and predict-then-check tasks so that 'current is the same all the way round a series loop' and 'voltage is a difference across something' are seen and measured rather than asserted. This topic is UK-anchored (KS3); NGSS has no equivalent middle-school expectation for DC-circuit current/voltage analysis.

activities.title: Two ammeters around one bulb: does current get used up?
feedback: If you predicted a smaller reading after the bulb, look again: both ammeters read the same, apart from tiny differences due to meter accuracy (e.g. 0.3 A before AND 0.3 A after). Current is not consumed.
What the bulb 'uses' is energy — that is where the 'using up' belongs, not in the current.
Moving the ammeter to any point in a single series loop gives the same reading; swapping the bulb for a buzzer does not change that the current is equal on both sides.

Adding a second identical bulb in series makes the current SMALLER everywhere than it was with one bulb (there is now more for the moving charge to pass through), but the reading is still equal at every point around the loop.
activities.rationale: The current-used-up/attenuation error is a persistent, widely reported difficulty. A predict-then-measure task with two meters makes the equal readings confront the prediction directly, and the committed pre-observation reason is the diagnostic. A moving-charge model makes conservation visible rather than told.
sourceClaims: The current-used-up / attenuation error and the current–voltage conflation are documented, persistent difficulties best addressed with a transport model (rope loop / moving charge) showing current is the same all the way round and voltage as energy per charge measured across a component.
learnerActions: Build (physically or in a circuit simulation) a single-cell, single-bulb series loop with one ammeter just BEFORE the bulb and an identical ammeter just AFTER it.
Before closing the switch, predict whether the second meter will read less than, equal to, or more than the first — commit to a specific value and write down your reason.
Close the switch and read both meters.
In a sim with visibly flowing charge, watch the dots stream round and note how quickly the dots pass a point (their speed) as a picture of the current.
Move one ammeter to a different point in the loop and read it again; try replacing the bulb with a buzzer and check whether the pattern holds.
Add a second identical bulb in series and read the ammeter again anywhere in the loop, saying what happened and why.
activities.intendedInsight: In a series circuit the current is the same all the way round: an ammeter reads the same before and after the bulb (within the accuracy of the meters). The bulb takes ENERGY, not charge — charge is conserved and simply circulates.

activities.title: Charges leave full, arrive empty: voltage as energy per charge
feedback: '3 V across the bulb' means each coulomb (unit) of charge transfers 3 joules of energy as it passes through the bulb.
Voltage is always a difference ACROSS two points — that is why a voltmeter bridges a component; a reading 'at one point' has no meaning on its own.
The cell gives energy to charge; the bulb takes energy from charge. The charge itself keeps flowing round — it is not made or destroyed.
Watch the energy of the charges drop across the component where the voltmeter reads a value: that is the energy being transferred there.
activities.rationale: Treating voltage as a flow, or as a property of a single point, is a core misconception. Grounding voltage as energy-per-charge and showing it as a difference across a component (with the cell loading and components unloading energy) explains the across-vs-through distinction physically.
sourceClaims: The current-used-up / attenuation error and the current–voltage conflation are documented, persistent difficulties best addressed with a transport model (rope loop / moving charge) showing current is the same all the way round and voltage as energy per charge measured across a component.
learnerActions: In the circuit model, snap a voltmeter ACROSS the cell and read it; then snap a voltmeter ACROSS the bulb and read it.
In a sim that shades charges by energy, watch charges leave the cell 'full/bright' and arrive back 'empty/dim' after unloading energy at the bulb.
Explain in your own words what a reading of, say, '3 V across the bulb' tells you about each bit of charge that passes through it.
Try connecting a voltmeter to a single point in the main line and describe what goes wrong or why it makes no sense.
Explain WHERE you would connect a meter to measure voltage and why there, rather than in the main line of flow.
activities.intendedInsight: Voltage (potential difference) is the energy transferred per unit charge — the energy the cell gives each bit of charge and the energy each component takes from it. Because it is a difference between two points, a voltmeter must straddle (go across) a component, not sit at one point.

activities.title: Where does each meter go, and why?
feedback: Correct placements: ammeter IN SERIES (in the line of flow, counting charge through), voltmeter IN PARALLEL (across a component, measuring the energy transferred per unit charge between those two points).
If both meters end up 'in the flow', that is the placement-confusion error: only current is measured through; voltage is measured across two points.
A voltmeter wrongly put in series tends to stop/choke the flow; an ammeter put across a component short-circuits it — the consequence tells you the rule.
Blanks: current is the rate of flow of CHARGE; voltage is energy per CHARGE.
activities.rationale: Placement errors are a symptom of not distinguishing through-flow (series) from difference-across (parallel). Tying placement to the reason, and letting wrong placements show their consequence, makes the rule meaningful rather than a ritual. Sorting/matching items surface the current-vs-voltage conflation directly, though they check recognition rather than producing an explanation.
sourceClaims: The current-used-up / attenuation error and the current–voltage conflation are documented, persistent difficulties best addressed with a transport model (rope loop / moving charge) showing current is the same all the way round and voltage as energy per charge measured across a component.
learnerActions: Sort a set of statements into two columns: 'about current' and 'about voltage' (e.g. 'measured in amperes', 'energy per charge', 'the same all the way round a series loop', 'a difference across a component', 'measured by a meter in series', 'measured by a meter in parallel').
Match each quantity to its unit and its instrument and its placement: current–ampere–ammeter–in series; voltage–volt–voltmeter–in parallel.
Look at circuit diagrams and spot the wrongly-placed meter (e.g. a voltmeter put in series, or an ammeter put across a component).
Try, in a sim that allows wrong placements, putting a voltmeter in series and an ammeter across a component, and describe the consequence you observe.
Fill in: 'current is the rate of flow of ___; voltage is energy per ___.'
Explain the reason behind each placement rule rather than reciting it.
activities.intendedInsight: An ammeter goes in series because it must be in the flow to count the charge passing through; a voltmeter goes in parallel because it compares the energy of charge on either side of a component — it measures a difference across. Sorting and matching can check whether the vocabulary and rules are recognised, but on their own they do not elicit the reasoning for WHY current stays constant while voltage drops; pair them with build/predict/measure and explanation.

activities.title: Currents add where branches meet
feedback: Check: the two branch readings should add up to the main-line reading where the branches meet.
Changing the cell voltage changes the size of the currents, but the branch currents still add to the main-line current.
This is the KS3 phrase 'currents add where branches meet' in action — charge splitting between paths, not disappearing.
activities.rationale: 'Currents add where branches meet' is explicit statutory KS3 content and reinforces charge conservation in a parallel context, extending the series-conservation insight. Measuring and summing branch currents makes the rule empirical rather than asserted.
sourceClaims: KS3 'Current electricity' statutory wording: electric current measured in amperes, in series and parallel circuits, currents add where branches meet, current as flow of charge; potential difference measured in volts; resistance measured in ohms as the ratio of p.d. to current.
learnerActions: Build (or simulate) a circuit with one branch point so the main line splits into two parallel paths and then rejoins.
Read the current in the main line and in each branch, and compare the main-line reading with the sum of the branch readings.
Adjust a slider for cell voltage (or add a cell) and re-read all the currents, describing what changes and what stays related.
State in your own words the rule for how branch currents relate to the main current where branches meet.
activities.intendedInsight: Where branches meet, the currents add: the current in the main line equals the sum of the currents in the branches. Current is conserved — it divides and recombines but is not lost.

activities.title: The battery sets the voltage; the circuit sets the current (analogy with caveats)
feedback: 'The battery supplies X amps whatever the circuit' is wrong: add more to the loop and the current changes even though the cell is the same.
Good analogy mapping: pump→cell, flow rate→current (A), pressure/push→voltage (V).

Where the water model breaks: a cut pipe spills water, but a broken wire does not spill charge — the current just stops; and the water picture does not show energy per unit charge well. (The wire being always 'full' of charge is a way the model fits, like a full sealed pipe — so don't picture charge draining away.)
More current does not automatically mean more voltage; they are distinct, and how they relate depends on resistance, which comes next.
activities.rationale: The 'fixed current from the battery' belief and the 'more current means more voltage' error both stem from not treating current and voltage as distinct quantities set by different things. Dialogue that probes predictions, plus an analogy used WITH stated limits, pre-empts these. The water/central-heating analogy is strong for current and pressure but silent/misleading on energy and leakage, so caveats matter.
sourceClaims: The current-used-up / attenuation error and the current–voltage conflation are documented, persistent difficulties best addressed with a transport model (rope loop / moving charge) showing current is the same all the way round and voltage as energy per charge measured across a component.
learnerActions: Discuss with a partner or an in-role 'electrician' the claim 'the battery always pushes out the same number of amps no matter what' — decide whether it is true and justify your view.
Use a water-circuit / central-heating picture: pump = cell, flow rate = current, pressure/push = voltage. Map each electrical quantity to its water counterpart.

List at least two places where the water analogy BREAKS (e.g. a cut pipe spills water, but a broken wire does not spill charge — the flow just stops; the water picture does not clearly show energy carried per unit charge). Note that 'the pipe/wire is always full' is where the analogy WORKS, not where it breaks.
Predict what happens to the current when you add more components to the loop, then check with meters.
State the summary rule: the cell provides voltage; the current depends on the whole loop (and, later, its resistance).
activities.intendedInsight: A cell does not force out a fixed current. It sets the voltage; the current that results depends on the whole circuit. Analogies help but have limits that must be named.

constraints: This topic is UK-anchored (KS3 Physics, Current electricity). NGSS has no middle-school performance expectation for DC-circuit current/voltage analysis; state the UK anchor honestly and do not imply NGSS coverage at this level.

Keep saying the three ideas explicitly and repeatedly: charge is the stuff that flows, current is how fast it flows (amperes), voltage is energy per charge (volts). Most errors collapse these into one 'electricity'.

Analogies (water circuit, rope loop) must carry explicit caveats: the rope loop shows current/conservation well but is silent on energy; the water model handles flow and pressure but breaks on leakage and on energy per charge. Never present an analogy as the full story.

Recognition and matching tasks (sorting statements, matching quantity–unit–instrument, spotting a mis-placed meter) check vocabulary and rules but do not by themselves elicit independent construction or reasoning about WHY current stays constant while voltage drops; pair them with build/predict/measure tasks and explanation.

A static labelled circuit diagram is a useful reference layer for vocabulary and correct meter placement, but it cannot display charge flowing at a rate, energy being delivered, or equal readings around a loop; use it as a pre-activity reference, not as the demonstration of conservation.
Predictions describe how an existing situation changes; have learners commit a value and reason BEFORE switching on so the equal readings can confront the prediction.
Allowing 'wrong' meter placements in a simulation is a learning-by-consequence device; make sure the consequence (choked flow / short) is visible and discussed, not left to chance.

Adding components such as bulbs or buzzers in series reduces the current everywhere in a single loop while keeping it equal at every point (an ideal ammeter or a closed switch added in series has negligible effect); voltage/current relationships via resistance are a later topic and should not be pre-asserted here beyond this observation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources have NOT been re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row's artefact-fit entries assert strong comparative/necessity claims ('Nothing static can show flow-rate conservation', '3D adds no purchase', a conversation 'targets the misconception through dialogue' but is 'weakly served by talk'). These comparative-efficacy and necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordances/limits in constraints rather than propagated as laws.
The IOP Spark source supporting the transport-model/misconception claim is marked verified:false in the row; treat that claim's support as unconfirmed.

The 'battery sets voltage / circuit sets current' principle in the final activity is physically sound but is not directly stated by any cited source claim; the attached IOP claim supports only the related current–voltage conflation strand ('more current means more voltage').
Specific current/voltage VALUES used in activities (e.g. 0.3 A, 3 V) are illustrative only and should be set by the actual circuit; do not present them as fixed outcomes.

The legacy reasoning is physically sound for this topic (series current conserved; voltage as energy per charge measured across; currents add at junctions; cell sets voltage, circuit sets current; added series components lower the current). No conceptual error required correction, but the quantitative relationship of current to voltage depends on resistance, a later topic that should not be pre-asserted here.

assess.poeTask: Build a series circuit with an ammeter just before the bulb and an identical ammeter just after it. Before closing the switch, ask the child to predict whether the second meter will read less than, equal to, or more than the first — commit to a value and a reason. Then switch on and read both. The current-consumed model predicts the 'after' meter reads lower; the equal readings force a rethink toward charge conservation, and the pre-observation reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If I add a second identical bulb in series, what happens to the ammeter reading anywhere in the loop — and why?
The voltmeter across the bulb reads 3 V. In your own words, what does '3 volts' tell us about each bit of charge that passes through?
Suppose I move the ammeter to the other side of the bulb — would you expect a different reading? What if the component were a buzzer instead of a bulb?
Where would you connect a meter to measure the voltage, and why there rather than in the main line?
assess.correctAnswer: The current is the same before and after the bulb — an ammeter reads the same on both sides. What the bulb 'uses' is energy: the voltage (potential difference) across the bulb drops because energy is transferred there. Current is the rate at which charge flows (amperes); voltage is the energy carried per unit charge (volts).

errorPatterns.pattern: Current-consumed model: 'the bulb uses up the current, so there's less current after it than before' — expects the ammeter to read lower on the far side.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put two ammeters, one each side of the bulb, and show equal readings; name what does drop (voltage/energy) so the child has somewhere to put the 'using up'.
errorPatterns.distractor: The current is smaller after the bulb because the bulb uses some of it up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tier-2 reasoning that has the current diminishing as it goes round, or predicting a lower reading on the ammeter after the bulb.

errorPatterns.pattern: Current/voltage conflation: uses 'current' and 'voltage' as two words for the same 'electricity' — 'the voltage flows through and gets used up, which is the same as the current dropping'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two with the analogy of rate-of-flow (amps, how much charge passes per second) versus energy-per-charge (volts); measure each with its own meter in its own place.
errorPatterns.distractor: The voltage flows through the bulb and gets used up, which is the same thing as the current dropping.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tier-2 explanation swaps the terms freely, or treats amps and volts as measuring the same thing.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ammeter/voltmeter placement confusion: puts both meters in the main line, or expects a voltmeter in series and an ammeter across the bulb.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tie placement to meaning: current is measured THROUGH (in series), voltage is measured ACROSS two points (in parallel) because it is a difference between them.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked (in follow-up) to place meters, connects the voltmeter in series or reasons that both meters go 'in the flow'.

responseLevels.gap: Says the current is used up in the bulb (smaller after it), or uses 'current' and 'voltage' interchangeably; would put both meters in the line.
responseLevels.full: Explains current as the conserved rate of charge flow (the same before and after the bulb) and voltage as the energy transferred per unit charge (which drops across the bulb), uses this to justify meter placement, and transfers the reasoning to a new component — coordinating the two quantities rather than listing them.
responseLevels.partial: Knows current is measured in amps and voltage in volts, and that an ammeter goes in series while a voltmeter goes in parallel, but recites these as separate facts — cannot say WHY current stays the same while voltage drops, or treats current and voltage as two names for the same 'electricity'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A single bulb is lit by one cell. Does the electric current get smaller after it has passed through the bulb, or is it the same all the way round the circuit? Explain your reasoning — and say what, if anything, the bulb actually 'uses up'.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding the current-consumed model, or conflating current with voltage, must predict the current is smaller after the bulb. The correct reasoner keeps current constant everywhere and moves the 'using up' onto energy/voltage. It is very hard to answer 'same all the way round, energy is what's transferred at the bulb' without the charge-flow-plus-energy model, and easy to get it wrong for the intuitive reason.
